---
title: "Marginal distributions"
---

The [preceding page](joint-probability.qmd) retained the paired values of two random variables. A marginal distribution removes one variable by summing or integrating over all of its values. Suppose a morphological analysis records tense $T$ and number $N$ for one sampled verb token.

| | singular $N=\mathrm{sg}$ | plural $N=\mathrm{pl}$ |
|---|---:|---:|
| past $T=\mathrm{past}$ | $.30$ | $.20$ |
| present $T=\mathrm{pres}$ | $.15$ | $.35$ |

The joint table preserves both distinctions. If our question concerns tense without retaining number, we must add over all number values.

The resulting one variable PMF is the [**marginal distribution**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html) of tense.

## Summing one row at a time

The past tense mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_T(\mathrm{past})
&=p_{T,N}(\mathrm{past},\mathrm{sg})
 +p_{T,N}(\mathrm{past},\mathrm{pl})\\
&=.30+.20\\
&=.50.
\end{aligned}
$$

The present tense mass is

$$
p_T(\mathrm{pres})=.15+.35=.50.
$$

Thus the marginal tense PMF is $(.50,.50)$.

The same operation down columns gives the marginal number PMF:

$$
p_N(\mathrm{sg})=.30+.15=.45
$$

and

$$
p_N(\mathrm{pl})=.20+.35=.55.
$$

## Adding the margins to the table

| | singular | plural | $p_T(t)$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| past | $.30$ | $.20$ | $.50$ |
| present | $.15$ | $.35$ | $.50$ |
| $p_N(n)$ | $.45$ | $.55$ | $1$ |

The term *marginal* comes from writing the resulting probabilities at the margins of a joint table.

## Stating the general operation

For discrete variables,

$$
p_T(t)=\sum_n p_{T,N}(t,n).
$$

Hold $T$ at the selected value $t$ and sum over every possible value of $N$.

For continuous variables,

$$
f_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$

The integral accumulates joint density across all $y$ while holding $x$ fixed.

Both operations remove one represented distinction while retaining a probability distribution over the other variable.

## Computing the margins in base R

```{r}
#| eval: false
joint_tense_number <- matrix(
  c(.30, .15, .20, .35),
  nrow = 2,
  dimnames = list(
    tense = c("past", "present"),
    number = c("singular", "plural")
  )
)

rowSums(joint_tense_number)
colSums(joint_tense_number)
```

The row sums give the tense margin; the column sums give the number margin.

## What marginalization changes

Marginalizing number answers how tense probability is allocated when number is not distinguished. It does not claim that number has no relationship with tense.

In the joint table, plural tokens are more often present than past, while singular tokens are more often past than present. Those pairings disappear from the tense margin $(.50,.50)$.

Marginalization is thus a deliberate loss of information, not a claim that the removed variable is scientifically irrelevant. It is appropriate when the target question averages across the removed variable; a conditional or joint question retains it.

## Check your understanding

1. Compute $p_N(\mathrm{pl})$ from the joint cells.
2. Verify that each marginal PMF sums to one.
3. Which joint information is lost when number is marginalized?
4. For continuous variables, which variable disappears in $f_X(x)=\int f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy$?

Marginalization removes a distinction. The [next page](conditional-independence.qmd) asks whether two variables remain associated after a third distinction is held fixed.
